name: Switch weapon mode
summary: One key swaps the unit's weapon for another, or the same weapon into a second fire mode, and the unit can move in both states (a swap into a state in which the unit cannot move at all is deploy-siege-mode; a mode that fires only while the unit stands still, such as the Hammer Tank's leech beam or a lock-on, stays here; one that also changes its body and movement is transform). The modes do different jobs: damage against a pin or tether beam, splash against a single heavy hit, a close spray against long precision, a quick shot against a slow lock-on that hits harder. Only one mode works at a time, so the player reads the fight and picks. The levers are how different the modes are, the swap time and any lockout, whether the swap is visible, and whether other abilities change with the mode.
counterplay: Read the active mode from its model, shots or icon, and fight it with what that mode is weak against.
Bring two different threats at once: it can answer only one of them in each mode.
Hit it during the swap, when neither mode is ready.
Against slow lock-on modes, keep moving or break line of sight: fast units slip out of the lock, and the Generals Missile Defender loses its lock if it moves.
Deny what a mode needs: a beam that needs the shooter standing still or a target in reach is broken by pressure or distance.

other_examples.note: Its anti-air weapon toggles between missiles that tear through groups of light fliers and heavy single-target cannons meant for big fliers such as carriers. It starts each life on the missiles and has to be ordered to switch.

After a barracks upgrade the rifleman can switch from his rifle to flash-bang grenades: a little more reach and a slower rate, with a blast that wipes out groups of infantry and empties a garrisoned building in one throw, but does nothing to vehicles or buildings. Unlike the rifle, the grenade can miss, because targets can step out of its landing spot while it flies.

The anti-tank soldier can switch on a laser sight that sharply raises his rate of fire and accuracy and adds a little reach, but each lock takes a few seconds before the first shot, and it breaks when the target dies or the soldier moves.

Switches its launcher to laser guidance: the lock takes longer, but the missiles fire much faster and reach further. Fast units simply move away before the lock completes, while buildings and slow units such as Kirov airships are easy prey; a patch fixed an exploit that kept the lock after the soldier moved.

Swaps his rifle for Molotov cocktails that can be thrown again and again from a good distance, burning out garrisons and shielded infantry. He can't swap while inside a building, so players send some Conscripts in with rifles and some with Molotovs.

Toggles its anti-armour main gun for a target painter that leaves the painted enemy taking much more damage from everyone; Red Alert 3 files this, like the Javelin's laser guidance, as a toggle-mode ability.

sources.title: Special ability (Red Alert 3), Command & Conquer Wiki
sources.note: Lists every unit's ability with the in-game button text.

shooter_analogues.note: The heavy Titan's tactical ability flips its minigun between a close-range spread and long-range precision rounds, and its ordnance changes with the mode: a knockback blast up close or a piercing explosive shot at range.

player_translation.summary: One key flips between two weapon modes with different jobs. The swap is quick but visible and briefly leaves neither mode ready, so the choice of mode is a running read of the fight: what is in front of me now, and what is coming next.
as_user: You carry two answers but use one at a time; good players switch before the fight changes, not after.

Typical pairs: a damage weapon and a pin or tether beam (the Terror Drone, the Hammer Tank), splash and a single heavy hit (the Thor), a close spray and long precision (Legion), a quick shot and a slow lock-on that pays off big (the Javelin).
A swap takes about half a second and each mode keeps its own ammo or heat, so swapping is never a free reload.
Some modes need conditions: a tether wants you still and the target in reach, a lock-on wants the target in view, so the strong mode costs mobility or time.
as_target: The active mode shows from above in the barrel model, the shot colour and a nameplate icon, so you know what it threatens.
Use the swap window: once you see it switch, you have a moment before the new mode is ready.
Against lock-on modes keep moving or break line of sight; against splash modes spread out; against a pin beam, have a teammate ready to punish the pinner.
teammates: A switcher fills whichever gap the team has right now and pairs well with specialists: it pins while others kill, paints a target for the team, or turns to anti-air when fliers show up.
Callouts matter: the HUD can tell allies which mode it is in.
The enemy team answers by showing two threats at once so it can only handle one.
controls: Left mouse fires whichever mode is active; Q switches mode. The pattern spends one counted key.
The second mode is not a separate secondary weapon on its own trigger, so right mouse stays free for the unit's secondary weapon or another ability.
Channelled modes (tether, painter) fire while left mouse is held and end on release, on a swap or when the target leaves reach.
feedback: A distinct model change per mode that reads from above (barrel, emitter, launcher) plus a colour-coded reticle and shot colour.
A mechanical clack on the swap and distinct firing sounds per mode.
HUD: both modes shown with the active one lit, swap progress and each mode's ammo or heat; enemies see the mode icon on the nameplate.
changes_from_rts: In the RTS the player orders a group to switch and the units then pick targets themselves; here the player aims, so the modes should differ in how they are aimed and used, not only in numbers.
RTS swaps are often free and instant; in a shooter an instant swap lets a skilled player always have the perfect answer, so add a short swap time and visible feedback.
The mode a unit spawns in should be the all-round one; the Thor's default to its missiles shows the RTS habit of starting in the common case.
Shooter weapon slots on number keys are separate weapons, not this pattern; this pattern is for modes that exclude each other and where switching is the decision.

Modes that the RTS lets fire only while standing still (the Hammer Tank must stand still to leech since patch 1.11) should slow the player heavily instead, so a mode choice never becomes a stand-still trap.

team_play.notes: Control or painter modes set up teammates' kills, and a switcher plugs the team's current gap; the enemy has to coordinate two threats at once to beat it.

notes: Two weapon definitions and a toggle, which most shooter weapon code already supports.
Each mode needs its own model or effect that reads from above, which is most of the work.
Edge cases: swapping mid-reload, mid-channel or mid-lock; ammo and heat per mode; what a stun does to a swap in progress.
A unit with two strong modes can answer everything; each mode needs a clear weakness, and the swap time is the main lever.
A free swap can cancel a reload or a recovery animation unless each mode keeps its own state.
Control modes (pins, tethers) combined with team damage can lock targets down; they need the same limits as any control effect.
Small barrel changes are invisible from a top-down camera, so colour, shot shape and an icon must carry the mode.
Enemies must see the switch happen, or every engagement feels like a coin toss.

variants.name: Damage or control
variants.summary: One mode deals damage, the other pins, slows or tethers the target while the unit's teammates do the killing.
variants.seen_in: Red Alert 3 Terror Drone (claws or stasis ray) and Hammer Tank (cannon or leech beam)

variants.name: Spread or focus
variants.summary: One mode covers an area or sprays close up, the other puts one heavy hit on one target or reaches far with precision.

variants.name: Lock-on mode
variants.summary: The strong mode has to lock on first, which takes a few seconds and breaks if the user moves or the target escapes, then fires faster and further.
variants.seen_in: Red Alert 3 Javelin soldier, Generals Missile Defender

adds_weaknesses.why: Its strong mode needs a few seconds to lock on and breaks if it moves or the target slips away.

variants.name: Special ammo
variants.summary: The same soldier or gun loads a second kind of shot with its own job, such as anti-garrison grenades or fire bombs, at the cost of what the first shot was good at.
variants.seen_in: Generals Ranger flash-bangs, Red Alert 3 Conscript Molotovs

variants.name: Painter mode
variants.summary: The second mode is a marker beam instead of a weapon: it does no damage itself but makes the painted target take more damage from the whole team.

variants.name: Kit follows the mode
variants.summary: Other abilities change with the mode too, so a close mode gets a close-range ability and a long mode a long-range one.
variants.seen_in: Titanfall 2 Legion (Power Shot changes with Mode Switch)

adds_strengths.why: Carries two answers and picks the one the fight needs.

adds_weaknesses.why: Only one mode works at a time, and each swap leaves a short gap with neither ready.

countered_by.why: Fast units change the fight faster than it can swap, and slip out of slow lock-on modes.
Blocking its abilities strands it in whichever mode it was in.

open_questions: Does each mode keep its own ammo or heat, so a swap is never a free reload? (Recommended: yes.)
Does a swap cancel a channel in progress, such as a tether, and reset a lock-on? (Recommended: yes to both.)
May a card's second mode be a tool (a repair beam, a painter) rather than a weapon? (Recommended: yes; the painter-mode variant does this.)
Should weapons ever cycle through three modes, or is two the limit for a top-down view? (Recommended: two.)

shooter_fit.reason: A familiar shooter mechanic (Titanfall's mode switch) that adds a quick, readable decision at little build cost; it needs strongly different modes to stay readable from above.

review.notes: Re-checked field by field against its sources by the batch r1 checker, which covered all 33 batch patterns; research/r1/checker/checks.json lists every field and verdict. Nothing was found wrong.
